question: To mark the International Day of Commemoration in Memory of the Victims of the Holocaust, the President of the Commission published a controversial video on the social media platform X, in which the names of a number of Holocaust victims were read out. Their birthplaces were juxtaposed with the places of their extermination in Europe.

It was stated in the video that Tekla Bruchsaler, a German national born in Duisburg, Germany, died in Auschwitz, Poland. This is an outright lie because Auschwitz was part of the territory annexed by Germany in October 1939, which, at the time, the occupiers themselves called Greater Germany. The Auschwitz concentration camp was set up on the basis of a decision taken by the German authorities in 1940.

I am pleased to see that, in response to widespread criticism, corrections have now been made to the film, which falsely suggested that German citizens had been exterminated on Polish territory. Unfortunately, however, the content makes no mention of the largest group of Holocaust victims: Polish citizens of Jewish origin.
The Commission’s message is an act of deliberate manipulation aimed at sharing among all Europeans the responsibility for the crimes of Nazi Germany and its collaborators.

There is an increasing need to repeat something that should be quite obvious: the Holocaust was the plan the Nazi Third Reich devised at the Wannsee Conference in Berlin and then put into practice in the terrorised territories that Germany had conquered around Europe, sometimes with the help of local collaborators. 1.
Does the Commission not think that in addition to removing the deceitful video, the Commission President should also apologise?

Does the Commission see a link between the policy of whitewashing the Germans’ responsibility for the Holocaust, the lack of proper education about German crimes, and the alarming rise of extremism in Germany, including antisemitic attitudes, as the President herself has reported?
answer: At the occasion of the International Holocaust Remembrance Day 2024, the Commission issued a video in which the Members of the College of Commissioners each read out the name of a victim of the Holocaust from their respective country. The original video referred to the Nazi extermination camp Auschwitz as located in ‘Auschwitz, Poland’, although Poland was at the time occupied by Nazi Germany.

The Commission recognised that this should have been specified. A revised version of the video was issued soon after replacing the incorrect one and referring to ‘German Nazi extermination camp’. It is essential to accurately portray historical events and locations, especially when addressing sensitive topics like the Holocaust.

Acknowledging and correcting mistakes ensures that the historical record is as accurate as possible, based on research, and shows respect for the victims and the survivors. There is an unprecedented spike in antisemitic acts all over Europe.

The Commission is committed to ensuring Holocaust education, research and remembrance as part of its EU Strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life (20212030) (1). The Commission is developing a ‘Network of Places Where the Holocaust Happened’ and launched a project to combat antisemitism in Europe through education (2). The EU emerged from the horrors of the World War II.

The Holocaust is a defining legacy of European history. Commemorating the Holocaust is EU’s joint responsibility and essential for understanding the values that underpin the EU today: respect of human dignity, fundamental rights, democracy and the rule of law.
